clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: The study used canonical correlation analysis (CCA) to identify multivariate associations between volumetric deviations (140 brain regions) and symptom severities (3 ADOS subscales). A novel algorithm called Random Forest with Homogeneous Canonical Correlation (RFHCC) was developed to identify subtypes with homogeneous brain-symptom associations, using split-half validation (10 repeats) to assess an index of homogeneity (Hs, range 0-10). Within each subtype, cross-loadings (correlations) between regional residuals and symptom scores were examined, reporting regions with |correlation| > 0.1 and p < 0.05 (uncorrected). For case-control classification, random forest classifiers were trained using volumetric deviations and CC-volume scores as features, with 60/40 train/test split repeated 100 times; performance evaluated by mean AUC. Permutation testing (1000 permutations) was used to assess whether subtyping significantly improved classification accuracy compared to random grouping. Kruskal-Wallis H tests compared demographics and symptoms across subtypes (FDR corrected). Sensitivity analysis regressed out age, gender, and TIV from canonical components to verify associations remained significant. Feature importance scores were computed using the eli5 package with 5-fold CV and 1000 shuffles.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Four ASD subtypes with distinct brain-symptom association patterns were identified, involving frontoparietal regions (subtype1), midbrain nuclei (subtype2), ventral visual pathway (subtype3), and anterior cingulate/pallidum (subtype4); subtyping improved case-control classification accuracy from 0.64 to 0.75 (p<0.05) and outperformed k-means clustering (0.68, p<0.01).
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Using the RFHCC algorithm on ABIDE data (N_controls=1146, N_ASD=571), four ASD subtypes were identified, each with distinct multivariate patterns of association between gray matter volume deviations and ADOS social symptom scores (all homogeneity indices Hs=10). Subtype1 (N=47): positive associations between greater ADOS-social severity and GMV overgrowth in frontoparietal regions (r=0.29-0.44), particularly right superior/inferior parietal gyrus, bilateral IFG, and right medial orbital gyrus; canonical correlation r=0.859 (p<0.001). Subtype2 (N=105): negative associations with midbrain structures (r=-0.31 to -0.20), particularly dorsal raphe nucleus and left VTA; canonical correlation r=-0.648 (p<0.001). Subtype3 (N=110): positive associations with ventral visual pathway (r=0.19-0.23), including left IOG/ITG and right MTG/fusiform; canonical correlation r=-0.757 (p<0.001). Subtype4 (N=92): negative associations with right ACC supracallosal, right pallidum, and IFG regions (r=-0.21 to -0.25); canonical correlation r=-0.697 (p<0.001). Subtypes differed significantly in age, gender ratio, and TIV (p<0.01) but not in symptom severity or IQ. Case-control classification using subtype-specific models achieved mean AUC=0.75 (range 0.64-0.91 across subtypes and matching algorithms), significantly better than without subtyping (AUC=0.64, p<0.05 by permutation test) and better than k-means clustering (mean AUC=0.68, p<0.01). Brain regions with strongest symptom associations also showed positive feature importance for classification in most subtypes (100% in subtype1, 93% in subtype2, 40% in subtype3, 17% in subtype4).

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Sample size limited by missing ADOS scores in ABIDE; midbrain nuclei (VTA, DRN) may be too small for accurate automated alignment; findings need validation in independent cohorts
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: First, the current approach based on the brain-symptom association required both neuroimaging measurements and symptom assessments, which limited the sample size used in this study owing to the missing data, especially the ADOS scores, in the ABIDE database. Future studies with larger sample sizes are needed for further validation of the subtyping. Second, the midbrain nuclei (e.g., VTA, DRN, etc.) might be too small to be mapped accurately onto individual brains by the automated alignment algorithm, so our findings for subtype 2 need to be interpreted with caution.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study developed a novel unsupervised algorithm (RFHCC - Random Forest with Homogeneous Canonical Correlation) that uses a tree-based splitting approach to identify patient subgroups with homogeneous multivariate brain-symptom associations. The algorithm employs an index of homogeneity (Hs) based on split-half cross-validation (10 repeats) to ensure association patterns replicate within subgroups. Dimensionality reduction via SVD was used to obtain grouping features (first 5 PCs explaining >80% variance). The algorithm grew 500 trees with depth up to 10, minimum node size of 40, and merged similar modes based on canonical weight correlation. Code is available at https://github.com/xdrzjj/ABIDE. Four different matching algorithms (EGMAD, MatchIt with optimal/knn/cardinality) were used to match controls to each subtype for case-control classification, demonstrating robustness across matching strategies.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This study is methodologically innovative in using normative modeling combined with a novel tree-based algorithm (RFHCC) to identify ASD subtypes based on homogeneous brain-symptom associations rather than purely neuroanatomical clustering. The canonical weights for ADOS subscales showed that only the social subscale had weight=1 in all subtypes, while communication and stereotyped behaviors subscales had weight=0, likely due to high inter-subscale correlations (p<1e-15). The study compared against k-means clustering and found superior classification performance with RFHCC. T-SNE analysis was used to verify that normative model residuals reduced site effects. Sensitivity analyses confirmed associations remained significant after controlling for age, gender, and TIV. The study excluded cerebellum and vermis from analysis based on prior literature showing no significant associations with ADOS symptoms or group differences. Sample sizes for subtypes were imbalanced (N=47 to 110), with subtype1 being smallest and subtype3 largest. After merging similar homogeneous modes, the final 4 subtypes were identified from an initial 9 homogeneous subgroups. The study used uncorrected p<0.05 for reporting regional associations (cross-loadings), which should be considered when interpreting regional findings.
